newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Asian central bankers mull virtual institution.
newsitem.headline: Asian central bankers mull virtual institution.

text.p: Asian central bankers are considering setting up a virtual institution instead of an actual physical institution to further tighten their cooperation, the chief executive of the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) said on Tuesday.

Joseph Yam, Hong Kong's de-facto central bank governor, said he was personally convinced by the arguments in favour of a virtual institution in a time of the Internet, but underscored it was still too early to tell what the bankers would decide.

Yam also told a briefing of the International Monetary Conference (IMC) that multi-lateral repurchase (repo) agreements among Asian central banks was being considered along with the creation of an institution to operate such facilities.
"I am convinced by the argument (for a virtual institution), although it is too early to tell," he said.
Yam said the Asian central bankers were committed to further increasing their cooperation, which recently helped counter the speculative attacks on the Thai bath.
"The trend of growing cooperation among these central banks will increase," Yam said.
Following Mexico's financial crises in late 1994, Asian central banks concluded a series of repo agreements to bolster their currencies in the event of an attack by markets.
Along with these agreements, there were proposals for setting up an institution -- an Asian-style Bank for International Settlements (BIS) -- to help shore up cooperation.
BIS is a forum for cooperation among central banks. Up until 1994 it was dominated by European central banks and their cooperation, but since then it has gradually become more global.
Yam said the spirit of the proposal for an Asian-style BIS was behind the increased cooperation among Asia's central banks.
"(The bilateral agreements) have been very useful and there is a consensus that we need to do more, to cooperate more," Yam said, adding:
"I can't be more specific on what we have got up our sleeves. It would be counterproductive to announce that before it is thought through," he said.

Yam confirmed that the 11 central banks grouped in the Executives Meeting of East and Asia Pacific (EMAP) central banks had been in close contact since their last meeting in Bangkok on May 25 and that they had intervened in markets to support the Thai currency.
"I can confirm we have been in the market, but not all of us," Yam said.
The bath came under speculative attack last month and the Thai central bank, the Monetary Authority of Singapore and other regional central banks jointly intervened to support the currency.
